items.text: Michigan splits 'bad faith' into three separate legal tools. Name them.

1) The MCL 500.2006 penalty-interest statute (privately enforceable). 2) The MCL 500.2026 unfair-practices list (DIFS-enforced only, no private suit). 3) Common-law bad faith, which Michigan recognizes only in the third-party duty-to-settle context, not for a first-party insured suing its own carrier.
Under MCL 500.2006(1), what must an insurer do, and what happens if it fails, unless the claim is reasonably in dispute?

The insurer must pay benefits on a timely basis to its insured, a person directly entitled to benefits, or a third party tort claimant, or in the alternative pay 12% interest on the late claim. Failing to do either is an unfair trade practice, unless the claim is reasonably in dispute.
An insurer neither pays a homeowner's fire claim on time nor pays any interest, and the claim was not reasonably in dispute. What has the insurer done under MCL 500.2006?
Committed an unfair trade practice under MCL 500.2006(1). The 'reasonably in dispute' language is the only escape from that label, and it is absent here.
Under MCL 500.2006(2), does an insurer commit an unfair trade practice merely by being found liable in court?
No. If the insurer pays the judgment plus the 12% interest required by subsection (4), it has not committed an unfair trade practice just because it was found liable.
How many days does an insurer have to specify in writing what constitutes a satisfactory proof of loss, under MCL 500.2006(3)?
30 days after receipt of the claim, unless the claim is settled within those 30 days.
A homeowner supplies a complete proof of loss on June 15. Under MCL 500.2006(3), by what date must the insurer pay the supported amount for the payment to count as timely?
Within 60 days after receipt of the proof of loss, roughly August 14.
MCL 500.2006(4) has two sentences. Who does the first sentence's 12% interest cover, and does it require the claim to be reasonably disputed first?
The insured or a person directly entitled to benefits under the insured's insurance contract. No reasonably-in-dispute qualifier appears in that first sentence at all.
For a third party tort claimant to get 12% interest under MCL 500.2006(4), what three things must be true?
The insurer's liability for the claim must not be reasonably in dispute, the insurer must have refused payment in bad faith, and a court of law must have determined that bad faith.
An insurer argues it owes no 12% interest to its own first-party insured because the claim was reasonably disputed. Correct?

No. The reasonably-in-dispute defense sits only in the second sentence of MCL 500.2006(4), which covers third-party tort claimants. Griswold (2007) and Nickola (2017) hold a first-party insured gets the 12% irrespective of dispute.
Under MCL 500.2006(4), what happens to interest owed under this section if the insurer separately owes interest on a judgment?
The interest paid under this section must be offset by any award of interest that is payable by the insurer as provided in the judgment.
An insurer offers to pay a claim, the claimant rejects the offer, and never recovers more than what was offered. Is interest still due under MCL 500.2006(4)?
No. If payment is offered by the insurer but rejected by the claimant, and the claimant does not subsequently recover an amount in excess of the amount offered, interest is not due.
What is the threshold preamble language of MCL 500.2026 for finding an unfair method of competition or deceptive act?

'Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the business of insurance, other than isolated incidents, are a course of conduct indicating a persistent tendency to engage in that type of conduct.'
Name the MCL 500.2026(1)(a) prohibited practice.
Misrepresenting pertinent facts or insurance policy provisions relating to coverages at issue.
Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection targets an insurer that never adopted reasonable standards for investigating claims?
Subsection (c): failing to adopt and implement reasonable standards for the prompt investigation of claims arising under insurance policies.
Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection targets denying a claim without a reasonable investigation of the available information?
Subsection (d): refusing to pay claims without conducting a reasonable investigation based upon the available information.
Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection covers failing to settle promptly once liability has become reasonably clear?
Subsection (f): failing to attempt in good faith to effectuate prompt, fair, and equitable settlements of claims in which liability has become reasonably clear.
An insurer offers a homeowner far less than the claim is worth, hoping to force a lawsuit. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection is this?
Subsection (g): compelling insureds to institute litigation to recover amounts due under an insurance policy by offering substantially less than the amounts due.

An adjuster requires a homeowner to submit a preliminary claim report and then makes them submit a full formal proof of loss for the sole purpose of duplicating a verification. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection describes this delay tactic?

Subsection (l): delaying the investigation or payment of claims by requiring an insured, claimant, or physician to submit a preliminary claim report and then requiring a subsequent formal proof of loss, seeking solely the duplication of a verification.

An insurer pays the undisputed dwelling portion of a claim late, on purpose, to pressure the homeowner into accepting less on the disputed contents portion. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection covers this?
Subsection (m): failing to promptly settle claims where liability has become reasonably clear under one portion of the policy coverage in order to influence settlements under other portions.
An insurer's denial letter says only 'not covered under the policy' with no cited provision or fact. Which MCL 500.2026(1) subsection does this violate?

Subsection (n): failing to promptly provide a reasonable explanation of the basis in the insurance policy, in relation to the facts or applicable law, for denial of a claim or offer of a compromise settlement.
A single insurance client has one bad claim experience with a carrier. Can DIFS bring a Chapter 20 enforcement action against the carrier based on that one file alone?

Not reliably. MCL 500.2026(1) requires 'other than isolated incidents ... a course of conduct indicating a persistent tendency.' Young v Michigan Mutual (1984) confirms a single client's dealings are, by nature, an isolated incident for this purpose, though that one file can still be evidence in a separate breach-of-contract or third-party bad-faith case.
Under MCL 500.2026(2), what record-keeping duty does an insurer have about complaints?

It must maintain a complete record of every complaint from its insureds since its last DIFS examination, showing total number, classification by line of insurance, nature, disposition, and processing time. Failing to keep that record is itself an unfair method of competition or deceptive act.
Under MCL 500.2028, when may the commissioner examine and investigate an insurer's affairs for unfair practices?
Upon probable cause, to determine whether the person has been or is engaged in an unfair method of competition or unfair or deceptive act or practice prohibited by sections 2001 to 2050.
Under MCL 500.2029, before a formal hearing notice issues, what opportunity must bureau staff give the person under investigation?

An opportunity to confer and discuss the possible complaint and proceedings informally with the commissioner or a representative; the matter may be disposed of summarily upon agreement of the parties at that stage.
At a Chapter 20 hearing under MCL 500.2030, who bears the burden of proof?
The agency (DIFS), or any intervenor who intervened in opposition to the person who is the subject of the proceeding, not the insurer or adjuster.
Under MCL 500.2030(3), if the subject of a Chapter 20 proceeding requests an independent hearing officer, how many peremptory dismissals of that officer may they exercise, and within what time?
One peremptory dismissal, exercised within 20 days after notification of the hearing officer's selection.
Under MCL 500.2038(1)(a), what is the maximum monetary penalty for an ordinary (non-knowing) Chapter 20 violation, per violation and in aggregate?
Not more than $1,000 for each violation, not to exceed an aggregate penalty of $10,000.
DIFS finds an insurer committed 3 Chapter 20 violations but did not know and had no reason to know it was violating the chapter. What is the maximum total monetary penalty under MCL 500.2038?
Not more than $1,000 per violation, capped at an aggregate of $10,000. Since it did not knowingly violate, the higher $5,000-per-violation / $50,000-aggregate tier does not apply.
An insurer knew, or reasonably should have known, it was violating Chapter 20, and did so repeatedly over a 6-month period. What is the maximum aggregate monetary penalty under MCL 500.2038?
Not more than $5,000 for each violation, not to exceed an aggregate of $50,000 for all violations committed in that 6-month period.
Besides monetary penalties, what two other remedies may the director order under MCL 500.2038(1)?
(b) Suspension or revocation of the person's license or certificate of authority, if the person knowingly and persistently violated the chapter, and (c) refund of any overcharges.
Under MCL 500.2040(1)(a), what is the maximum monetary penalty for violating a cease-and-desist order that is already in effect?
Not more than $20,000 for each violation, in addition to possible suspension or revocation of license or certificate of authority.
Can a Chapter 20 cease-and-desist order under MCL 500.2040(3) impose fines for conduct that happened before the order was issued?
No. A cease-and-desist order must not contain fines or other penalties applicable to acts or omissions that occur before the date of the order.
What did Young v Michigan Mutual Ins Co, 139 Mich App 600 (1984), hold about a private tort claim based on MCL 500.2006?
'There is no implied private cause of action in tort for violation of MCL 500.2006.' A private party cannot sue in tort for a violation of the prompt-pay statute.
In Young v Michigan Mutual, what did the court say about an independent cause of action under MCL 500.2026?

Quoting Shavers v Attorney General, the court held isolated incidents do not constitute unfair trade practices under MCL 500.2026 (a single client's dealings are necessarily isolated); MCL 500.2026 gives the Commissioner of Insurance authority over continuing practices, and 'the insured does not have an independent cause of action' under it.
Young v Michigan Mutual bars a tort suit under MCL 500.2006. Does that also mean an insured cannot directly collect the statute's 12% interest at all?

No. Young itself notes prior Michigan case law (Fletcher v Aetna Casualty) already let a private party 'directly recover the interest penalty' under 2006. What is barred is framing that recovery as an independent tort claim, not the ordinary statutory interest claim.
What is the actual holding of Kewin v Massachusetts Mutual Life Ins Co, 409 Mich 401 (1980)?

'We decline to follow the California court and to declare the mere bad-faith breach of an insurance indemnity contract an independent and separately actionable tort.' Michigan does not recognize a first-party bad-faith tort; the claim sounds in contract only.
In Kewin, how did the court distinguish Harbaugh (where a tort claim succeeded) from the insurance-contract bad-faith claim before it?

Harbaugh involved a duty imposed by statute, existing 'independent of and apart from the contractual undertaking.' In Kewin, the only duty came from the contract itself, so under Hart v Ludwig, breaching it 'is not a duty imposed by the law upon all' and 'a tort action will not lie.'
TRAP: Does the exact phrase 'wholly separate and independent' appear in the Kewin opinion?

No. That four-word phrase is not found anywhere in the full Kewin opinion text. Kewin's actual quoted holding refuses to make bad-faith breach 'an independent and separately actionable tort.' The 'wholly separate and independent' phrasing traces to a later gloss, not to Kewin itself.
What is the controlling definition of 'bad faith' from Commercial Union Ins Co v Liberty Mutual Ins Co, 426 Mich 127 (1986)?
'Arbitrary, reckless, indifferent, or intentional disregard of the interests of the person owed a duty.' This is the third-party duty-to-settle standard, not a first-party rule.
According to Commercial Union v Liberty Mutual, can bad faith exist without actual dishonesty or fraud?

Yes. Because bad faith is a state of mind, if the insurer is 'motivated by selfish purpose or by a desire to protect its own interests at the expense of its insured's interest, bad faith exists,' even without dishonesty. But good-faith denials, honest errors of judgment, and mere negligence are not enough.
How many non-exclusive factors did Commercial Union v Liberty Mutual list for a jury to weigh on third-party bad faith, and are any of them decisive alone?

12 factors, and 'no single factor shall be decisive.' They include things like failing to keep the insured informed, failing to accept a reasonable within-limits settlement offer, and failing to properly investigate before refusing a within-limits offer.

A liability insurer rejects a reasonable settlement offer within policy limits, refuses to inform its insured of the offer, and ignores its own adjuster's advice to settle. Under Commercial Union's 12 factors, is this evidence of bad faith?
Yes. All three actions match listed factors: rejecting a reasonable within-limits offer, failing to inform the insured of settlement offers, and disregarding the advice of an adjuster or attorney.
Commercial Union v Liberty Mutual warns against judging an insurer's conduct with '20-20 hindsight.' What does that mean in practice?
Conduct must be judged by the circumstances existing at the time of the decision, not evaluated years later with the benefit of knowing how the underlying case actually turned out.
What did the special conflict panel hold in Griswold Properties LLC v Lexington Ins Co, 276 Mich App 551 (2007)?
'A first-party insured is entitled to 12 percent penalty interest if a claim is not timely paid, irrespective of whether the claim is reasonably in dispute.'
What did the Michigan Supreme Court hold in Nickola v MIC General Ins Co, 500 Mich 115 (2017), about an insured's own UIM claim?

An insured making a claim under his or her own policy for underinsured-motorist benefits cannot be considered a 'third party tort claimant' under MCL 500.2006(4); the reasonably-in-dispute exemption in the second sentence does not apply to that claim.
Nickola overruled which prior Court of Appeals opinion, and held its rule consistent with which other published case?
It overruled Auto-Owners Ins Co v Ferwerda Enterprises, Inc (On Remand) to the extent inconsistent, and held its rule 'entirely consistent with ... the Court of Appeals' opinion in Griswold.'
Smith v Globe Life Ins Co, 460 Mich 446 (1999), held two things about the MCPA and insurance. What were they, and what happened to the MCPA count?

One: MCL 445.904(1)(a) does exempt the sale of insurance, because the test is 'whether the general transaction is specifically authorized by law, regardless of whether the specific misconduct alleged is prohibited.' Two: the version of section 4(2) then in force carved a private section 11 action back out of that exemption, so the MCPA count survived. The Court held 'defendant is not entitled to summary disposition of plaintiff's mcpa claims' and remanded. Smith did NOT hold that the MCPA never reaches insurance.
What does current MCL 445.904(3) say about MCPA claims based on Chapter 20 conduct occurring on or after March 28, 2001?

The Michigan Consumer Protection Act 'does not apply to or create a cause of action' for an unfair, unconscionable, or deceptive practice made unlawful by Chapter 20 of the Insurance Code, if the conduct occurred on or after March 28, 2001. That date is the effective date of 2000 PA 432 in the section's history; subsection (3)'s current wording was set by 2014 PA 251, made retroactive to March 28, 2001.
What does the general exemption in MCL 445.904(1)(a) cover?

The Consumer Protection Act does not apply to 'a transaction or conduct specifically authorized under laws administered by a regulatory board or officer acting under statutory authority of this state or the United States.'
A homeowner today tries to sue their insurer under the Michigan Consumer Protection Act for conduct that would violate MCL 500.2026. Does the claim survive?
No. MCL 445.904(3) bars an MCPA claim resting on conduct made unlawful by Chapter 20 of the Insurance Code, for conduct occurring on or after March 28, 2001, which covers any current claim.
What would Senate Bill 245 of 2025 do to Chapter 20, and what is its status as of this run?

It would amend MCL 500.2005, 500.2006, 500.2026, and 500.2049, and add MCL 500.2005b plus a new Chapter 30B creating a private civil cause of action against insurers for violations of sections 2006, 2026, and 2027. Status: reported favorably from committee June 17, 2026, referred to the Committee of the Whole June 18, 2026. It has not passed either chamber and is not law.
Can a public adjuster or attorney cite Senate Bill 245's proposed private bad-faith cause of action in a demand letter as current Michigan law?

No. SB 245 is a pending bill, not enacted. Its proposed Chapter 30B, titled 'RIGHT TO A CIVIL CAUSE OF ACTION AGAINST INSURERS FOR CERTAIN CONDUCT,' would let a person damaged by a violation of section 2006, 2026, or 2027 sue the insurer, with punitive and emotional-distress damages on a bad-faith finding and a rebuttable presumption of bad faith from a 2026 or 2027 violation. None of that is law. The current rule is Kewin (no first-party bad-faith tort) plus MCL 500.2006's 12% penalty interest.
What does DIFS Bulletin 2025-25-INS (October 24, 2025) address, and which MCL 500.2026 subsections does it quote?

'Improper Claims Administration Practices in Automobile Insurance.' It quotes MCL 500.2026(1)(c) (reasonable investigation standards) and (f) (prompt, fair, equitable settlement once liability is reasonably clear), and lists sanctions of fines and/or suspension or revocation of certificate of authority.
How does Michigan's first-party bad-faith framework compare to Florida's?

Florida has a real statutory first-party bad-faith cause of action: Fla. Stat. section 624.155, titled 'Civil remedy,' lets 'any person' sue an insurer for, among other things, 'not attempting in good faith to settle claims.' It requires 60 days' pre-suit notice, and since 2022 section 624.1551 bars a residential property bad-faith action until the insured wins an adverse adjudication that the insurer breached the contract. Michigan has no equivalent: no first-party bad-faith statute and no first-party bad-faith tort. The insured's tools are the 12% penalty interest, ordinary breach damages, and DIFS complaints. This is a labeled contrast, never a Michigan argument.
In Kewin, what did the insured actually walk away with, and what happened to the mental-distress and exemplary-damages awards?

Contract benefits only. The Court affirmed the awards of $16,500 for breach of the disability policy and $798.40 on the companion life policy, affirmed the Court of Appeals' reversal of the mental or emotional distress award, and reversed and set aside the $50,000 exemplary-damages award. Justice Kavanagh wrote for the majority; Justice Williams wrote separately and would have allowed emotional-distress contract damages, but that view did not command the Court.
